newsitem.title: USA: Corn, soybeans drop on rain forecast, gasoline up.
newsitem.headline: Corn, soybeans drop on rain forecast, gasoline up.

text.p: A forecast for more rains in parched areas of the Midwest this week pushed corn and soybean prices down on Thursday.

In other markets, gasoline prices rose on worries about supply disruptions due to a storm in the Gulf of Mexico, and gold prices rose as speculators took a break from recent heavy selling to take profits.
At the Chicago Board of Trade, soybeans for July delivery closed 7-1/2 cents a bushel lower at $7.74-1/2 and corn for July delivery fell one cent a bushel to $2.65-1/2.
"Weather continues to be the dominant feature out here," said Mark Weidner, an analyst with Cargill Investor Services.
"The majority of the trade's belief is that next week's system is going to be able to tap into the Gulf moisture."

Fred Gesser, forecaster for Omaha-based Weather Express Inc., said rains pushing northward from a tropical storm in the Gulf of Mexico would soon soak Illinois. Recent rains bypassed central Illinois, a key growing region.

"Moisture from what should become Tropical Storm Danny is in a position to provide one-half to two-plus inches with 80 percent coverage for Missouri and southern Illinois up to Peoria on Monday," Gesser said.
"The weather basically has broken and it doesn't look like we'll have a problem," said Charlie Sernatinger, analyst for E.D. and F. Man International.
July soybeans were also pressured by talk that a major commercial firm would deliver cash soybeans against the contract before it expires on July 22.

Wheat prices closed steady, with July futures unchanged at $3.25 a bushel. But traders were perplexed by news during the day by a statement from the Egyptian government barring imports of genetically altered crops.

Egypt is a major buyer of world wheat, a crop not yet widely affected by plant genetics. But it also buys corn and soybeans, which are increasingly being produced from plants genetically altered to resist disease or insects.

"We're pressing for a meeting on Monday," said Timothy Galvin of the U.S. Agriculture Department's Foreign Agricultural Service. "We're not worried but very concerned and that's why we're trying to meet with Eyptian agriculture officials."

Gasoline prices at the NYMEX ended sharply higher on concerns that Tropical Storm Danny could disrupt refinery operations in the Gulf of Mexico when supplies of a key gasoline blending component are already tight.
August gasoline settled 1.43 cents higher at 61.89 cents a gallon.

"Gasoline rose today because of news of the storm. The MTBE price continues to outpace RFG, which is an old story now, and the trade has accumulated large long positions as a result," said Todd Miller, a trader with Morgan Stanley.
MTBE is a key blending component in the reformulated gasoline (RFG) grade deliverable against the NYMEX contract.
Gasoline pushed the rest of the oil complex higher, with August crude ending up 34 cents at $19.99 a barrel and August heating oil finishing up 1.21 cents a gallon at 53.89 cents.
Precious metals prices ended higher led by a jump in gold prices, with gold for August delivery at the COMEX in New York closing up $6.00 an ounce at $324.70, its highest level in 10 days.

"Gold has been technically oversold for some time now," said Scott Mehlman, Credit Lyonnais Rouse's New York chief bullion dealer. "Today's move appeared to be triggered by breaches of minor resistance around $321 and then $324, but August gold still has to get back up through major resistance around $325.00 to set off a big rally," he said.
"In the meantime, the brave will sell it again and probably be rewarded, but it won't be easy tomorrow," he said.

Gold was fixed at a 12-year low last week at $315.75 in London after news of a sale of 167 metric tons of gold by the Reserve Bank of Australia, which encouraged massive amounts of extra selling by speculators.

September silver at COMEX ended up 6.00 cents at $4.245 an ounce, buoyed by the rise in gold. October platinum at the New York Mercantile Exchange closed up $1.50 an ounce at $393.70 and September palladium ended up $2.70 at $160.35.
Russian shipments of palladium to Japan resumed this week after a six-month suspension, but problems appear to be developing with shipments of platinum, which have not arrived yet, traders said.
